source.title: The $\varphi$ Curve: The Shape of Generalization through the Lens of Norm-based Capacity Control
source.authors: Yi-Chen Wang; Yu-Dong Chen; L. Rosasco; Fang-Hui Liu

record.file_problem: The paper text is present in full. Some extracted figures, especially in Section H.4, are garbled, so exact plotted values cannot be recovered; the accompanying prose remains readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own model-size and norm-based-capacity results and argues that the apparent double-descent shape depends on the capacity measure. It refines the claim rather than simply reproducing the original experiments.
record.gate_note: Rows include the paper’s own model-size, sample-size-scaling, noise-level, and risk-versus-norm results. The introductory curve attributed to prior lecture notes and results attributed to cited papers are not treated as this study’s results. The epoch-wise claim is not tested: training epochs are specified for some experiments, but no test-risk-versus-epoch result is reported.
record.test_reason: The paper's own theory and experiments argue that double descent disappears when risk is plotted against the estimator's ℓ2 norm (random-feature models) or path norm (neural nets), and they report their own model-size sweeps. This is a direct, argued restatement bearing on V7, with own-result reproductions bearing on V1, V4 and V6. The ResNet18/CIFAR-10 run reproduces the original deep double-descent setup.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. For random-feature and linear models, risk against the estimator's ℓ2 norm shows a phase transition between under- and over-parameterization but no double descent, and is closer to a classical U shape. Path norm in neural nets behaves similarly, and the authors call double descent transient. They also report that effective dimension, degrees of freedom, Frobenius norm and spectral complexity still show double descent. They say real data can give a φ-curve their theory does not fully capture.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops deterministic-equivalent theory for ℓ2 estimator norms in linear and random-feature regression and adds experiments on neural networks; it is not a direct reproduction of the original method. The paper also says it includes replication materials for OpenAI’s deep double-descent results.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported shape depends on the capacity measure (parameter count versus estimator ℓ2 norm or neural-network path norm), the under- versus over-parameterized regime, data assumptions or dataset, and label-noise level. In the random-feature experiments, regularization level and activation function are also varied.

fits_no_version.finding: In random-feature ridge regression with p=n^q and λ=n^-(ℓ-1), risk scales as n^γn·N^γN with γn≤0 in all regions. γN is positive when p is large and negative when p is small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling laws written in norm-based capacity are not monotone in capacity: risk can rise or fall with the norm depending on the regime.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed p, varying λ gives a U-shaped risk-vs-norm curve (L-curve) in both under- and over-parameterized regimes (Fig. 2(d), 8, 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tuning regularization traces a U-shaped risk-versus-norm curve at fixed model size.

record.peer_reviewed: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025)
record.problems: The core theory is for linear and random-feature models, and the neural-network evidence covers selected architectures and datasets. Several results are described qualitatively rather than with readable numeric values because extracted figures are garbled. The authors note that their assumptions may not hold for some real-world data; the non-asymptotic bias result for random-feature norms is presented as informal and not fully proved. The neural-network experiments report means and standard deviations for some settings, but do not provide readable numerical values here.
record.rows_left_out: No cited results or the introductory curve attributed to lecture notes were included. No epoch-wise outcomes were reported. Figure-only details were omitted where the accompanying text did not specify a result or where the extracted plots were unreadable.

untested.parts: No test error versus epochs is reported.
No sample-size sweep at a fixed model near the interpolation threshold.
No single complexity measure is tested as predicting peak location across size, epochs and samples.
Multiple or triple peaks are not tested. Whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak is not reported in the risk-vs-p sweeps.
Only linear and random-feature regression are examined among non-deep classes; trees, kernels and other classes are not.
Exact peak locations relative to the training-set fitting point are not readable for the MLP, CNN and ResNet18 runs.

missing.what: Double descent persists when risk is plotted against degrees of freedom df1/df2 in linear ridge regression
Double descent persists against Frobenius norm and spectral complexity in the two-layer net; Frobenius distance is uninformative
Against the first-layer Frobenius norm in random-feature models, the curve is a reshaped double descent
FashionMNIST ridgeless random features give a φ-curve (over-parameterized branch initially above the under-parameterized one); Gaussian synthetic data keep it strictly below
Linear regression risk-vs-norm: linear relation under-parameterized, rectangular hyperbola over-parameterized (isotropic features)

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this paper. The ResNet18 run is a T1-style replication of V1. The V3 label was dropped because R6 is a joint n-p-λ scaling theory, not a sample sweep near the threshold. The non-asymptotic bias result for random-feature norms is stated as informal (unproved).

versions.untested_parts: The text describes double descent with model size in neural networks, but does not provide readable numerical peak locations relative to the exact point at which each network first fits its training set.
Test error over training epochs is not reported.

The reported scaling-law result varies sample size under jointly specified parameter-count and regularization scaling; it does not isolate increasing sample size at a fixed setting precisely near the interpolation threshold.
The evidence covers linear and random-feature models and selected neural-network families, not all model classes.
The study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample-size axes.

The paper reports stronger double-descent peaks at higher label-noise levels in two-layer neural networks. It does not test multiple or triple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization makes peaks disappear.
The paper compares parameter-count curves with ℓ2- or path-norm curves, but does not establish that the second descent becomes an ordinary single U-shaped curve across all regimes.
